The trough is an **extreme** position, and a quarter of a period separates an extreme
from the mean position.
**Step 1 — recall the four stages of a cycle.** Starting from the mean position, a
particle in simple harmonic motion goes
mean → **crest**: T/4
crest → mean: T/4
mean → **trough**: T/4
trough → mean: **T/4** ✓
and the whole cycle takes T.
**Step 2 — apply it.** A particle at the trough reaches the mean position after
**T/4** ✓
**The algebra, to confirm.** With y = −A cos ωt starting at the trough:
y = 0 when cos ωt = 0, that is ωt = π/2
t = (π/2)/(2π/T) = **T/4** ✓
**What the particle is doing there.** At the trough it is momentarily **at rest**, with
maximum displacement and maximum acceleration ✓ At the mean position a quarter period
later it has **maximum speed**, ωA, and **zero** acceleration - the two states are
exact opposites.
**The energy at each point.**
trough: all **potential**, ½kA² ✓
mean: all **kinetic**, ½mω²A² ✓
and the two are numerically equal, as energy conservation requires.
**A caution about the particle's motion.** In a transverse wave each particle moves
only **up and down** ✓ It does not travel along with the wave - the **disturbance**
advances, not the medium.
**The companion question.** Trough to **crest** takes **T/2**, since the particle must
cross the mean position on the way ✓ which is why T/2 is offered as the first
distractor.
**A worked instance.** For a wave of frequency 50 Hz, T = 0·02 s, so the journey from
trough to mean takes **5 ms** ✓
**Why the wavelength does not enter.** The question is about the **time** a single
particle takes, which depends only on the period ✓ The wavelength would matter for
comparing **different** particles along the wave.
**Reading the distractors.** **T/2** ✗ is trough to crest. **T** ✗ is a complete cycle,
returning to the trough. **2T** ✗ is two cycles ✓
∴ T/4.

The optical rotation measures how much **actual sugar** is present; compare that with the
total.
**Step 1 — apply the polarimeter relation.**
θ = S l c ✓
with θ the rotation, S the specific rotation, l the tube length and c the concentration
of the optically active substance.
**Step 2 — convert the tube length.**
20 cm = **0·2 m** ✓
**Step 3 — solve for the sugar concentration.**
c = θ/(S l)
= 19/(0·5 x 0·2)
= 19/0·1
= **190 kg m⁻³** ✓
**Step 4 — find the purity.** The solution holds 200 kg m⁻³ of impure sugar, of which
190 is actually sugar:
purity = 190/200
= **95%** ✓
**Why the impurity contributes nothing.** Only **optically active** substances rotate
the plane of polarisation ✓ The 10 kg m⁻³ of impurity adds mass but no rotation - which
is exactly what makes polarimetry a purity test.
**Why sugar rotates the plane.** Its molecules are **chiral** - they have no plane of
symmetry and exist in left- and right-handed forms ✓ Natural sucrose is
**dextrorotatory**, turning the plane clockwise as seen by the observer.
**Where this is used.** Sugar refineries, customs laboratories and the food industry
test purity exactly this way ✓ The instrument is called a **saccharimeter**, and the
specific rotation of sucrose is a tabulated standard.
**Why a longer tube helps.** The rotation is proportional to the path length ✓ so dilute
solutions are measured in long tubes to get a readable angle. A 20 cm tube is standard.
**A check on the units.**
[S l c] = (deg m² kg⁻¹)(m)(kg m⁻³) = **degrees** ✓ consistent, and a useful guard
against forgetting to convert centimetres to metres - which would give c = 19 kg m⁻³
and a nonsensical purity of under 10%.
**Reading the distractors.** **20%** ✗ is the figure one gets by leaving l in
centimetres and then mis-forming the ratio - and it is also the **impurity** read as a
purity. **80%** ✗ and **89%** ✗ correspond to concentrations of 160 and 178 kg m⁻³,
neither of which satisfies θ = Slc ✓
∴ 95 %.

The electric force between **vertical** plates is **horizontal**, so it combines with
gravity in **quadrature**.
**Step 1 — identify the two forces on the bob.**
gravity: **mg**, vertically down
electric: **qE**, **horizontally** - because the plates are vertical, the field between
them is horizontal ✓
**Step 2 — combine them.** Being perpendicular, they add by Pythagoras:
F_eff = √[(mg)² + (qE)²] ✓
**Step 3 — find the effective gravity.**
g_eff = F_eff/m
= **√[g² + (qE/m)²]** ✓
**Step 4 — write the period.**
T = 2π√(l/g_eff)
= **2π√{l/√[g² + (qE/m)²]}** ✓
**Why the forces add in quadrature and not simply.** They are at **right angles** ✓
Adding or subtracting qE/m from g - as two of the distractors do - would be right only
if the plates were **horizontal**, making the electric force vertical.
**Where the pendulum now hangs.** Not vertically, but tilted towards one plate by
tan α = qE/(mg) ✓ The bob oscillates about that new equilibrium direction, and the
effective gravity points along it.
**Why the period is always shortened.** g_eff = √(g² + something²) is **greater** than
g whatever the sign of the charge ✓ so the pendulum always runs **faster** between
charged vertical plates - and reversing the field changes which way it leans, but not
the period.
**A worked instance.** With qE/m = 0·75g:
g_eff = g√(1 + 0·5625) = **1·25g** ✓
so T falls to T₀/√1·25 = **0·894 T₀**, and the bob hangs at tan⁻¹(0·75) = **36·9°** from
the vertical.
**The companion case.** With **horizontal** plates the field is vertical, and
g_eff = g ± qE/m ✓ The period then lengthens or shortens according to the sign of the
charge - and those are precisely the second and third options, included to test whether
the plate orientation has been read.
**The general principle.** In any uniform additional force field, replace g by the
**resultant acceleration** and measure l along the new equilibrium direction ✓ The same
trick handles a pendulum in an accelerating lift, in a car rounding a bend, or in a
rocket.
∴ 2π√{l/√[g² + (qE/m)²]}.

Halving the period means **quadrupling** the effective gravity.
**Step 1 — write the two periods.**
at rest: T = 2π√(l/g) ✓
accelerating upward at a: T′ = 2π√[l/(g + a)] ✓
**Step 2 — impose the condition.**
T′ = T/2
so
2π√[l/(g + a)] = ½ x 2π√(l/g)
**Step 3 — square both sides and cancel.**
1/(g + a) = (1/4)(1/g)
g + a = **4g**
**a = 3g** ✓
**Why the factor is four and not two.** The period depends on the **square root** of the
effective gravity ✓ To halve T, g_eff must be multiplied by 2² = **4** - and since g is
already present, only **3g** of extra acceleration is needed.
**Why upward acceleration shortens the period.** The lift's floor pushes harder, so the
bob behaves as though gravity were stronger ✓ The restoring force is greater and the
swing quicker - the pendulum clock in an accelerating lift runs **fast**.
**The four cases, for completeness.**
at rest or constant velocity: g_eff = **g** ✓
accelerating **up** at a: g_eff = **g + a**, period shorter ✓
accelerating **down** at a: g_eff = **g − a**, period longer
**free fall**, a = g: g_eff = **0**, so T → **∞** - the pendulum does not swing at all ✓
**How large 3g is.** Nearly **30 m s⁻²** ✓ no real lift accelerates like that; the
passenger would feel four times their own weight. The question is an exercise in the
formula.
**A check.** With g_eff = 4g:
T′ = 2π√(l/4g) = ½ x 2π√(l/g) = **T/2** ✓
**Why the length and mass never appear.** Only the **ratio** of the periods is asked
for, and both l and m cancel ✓ The mass of the bob never enters a pendulum's period at
all.
**Reading the distractors.** **g** ✗ gives g_eff = 2g and T′ = T/√2 = 0·707T. **2g** ✗
gives T/√3 = 0·577T. **4g** ✗ gives T/√5 = 0·447T ✓ Only 3g makes g_eff exactly four
times g.
∴ 3 g.

Read the wave number off the equation and multiply by the separation.
**Step 1 — identify k.** Comparing
y = 6 sin 2π(2t − 0·1x)
with the standard form y = A sin(ωt − kx):
k = 2π(0·1)
= **0·2π rad mm⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the phase-difference formula.**
Δφ = k Δx
= (0·2π)(2)
= **0·4π radians** ✓
**Step 3 — convert to degrees.**
0·4π x (180/π) = 0·4 x 180
= **72°** ✓
**The wavelength, as a check.**
λ = 2π/k = 2π/(0·2π) = **10 mm** ✓
and a separation of 2 mm is **one fifth** of a wavelength, so the phase difference is
one fifth of 360° = **72°** ✓ the same answer, and the quickest route.
**The relation worth remembering.**
**Δφ/2π = Δx/λ** ✓
phase difference is to a full cycle as the path difference is to a wavelength. Every
interference and diffraction calculation rests on it.
**Reading the rest of the wave.**
amplitude: **6 mm**
frequency: 2π(2t) means ω = 4π, so f = **2 Hz** ✓
speed: v = fλ = 2 x 10 = **20 mm s⁻¹**
period: **0·5 s**
**Why the units stay in millimetres.** Both x and λ are in mm, and only their **ratio**
enters ✓ Converting to metres would work equally well, provided both are converted.
**Why the "at any instant" matters.** The phase difference between two fixed points is
**constant in time** ✓ Both particles oscillate at the same frequency, so they maintain
a steady 72° relationship for ever - which is what makes them coherent.
**A landmark to calibrate against.** Points **half a wavelength** apart - 5 mm here -
are **180°** out of phase, moving in exactly opposite directions ✓ Our 2 mm is less than
that, so the answer must be under 180°, which rules out nothing here but is a useful
sanity check.
**Reading the distractors.** **36°** ✗ is the phase difference for 1 mm. **18°** ✗ for
0·5 mm. **54°** ✗ for 1·5 mm ✓ All follow from the same formula with the wrong
separation.
∴ 72°.

A wavefront is a surface of constant **phase**.
**Step 1 — state the definition.** A wavefront is the locus of all points of a medium
that are vibrating **in the same phase** ✓ - all at a crest together, or all at a trough
together, or all passing through the mean position in the same direction.
**Step 2 — see the consequence.** Since every point on it is in step, the wavefront
moves forward as a unit, and the **rays** - the directions of travel - are everywhere
**perpendicular** to it ✓
**The shapes wavefronts take.**
a **point source**: **spherical** wavefronts, expanding outwards ✓
a **line source**: **cylindrical**
a source at **infinity**, or a collimated beam: **plane** ✓
**Why not amplitude.** The amplitude **falls off** with distance from the source - as
1/r for a spherical wave - so points on a single wavefront share a phase but not
necessarily an amplitude ✓ In an absorbing or spreading medium the amplitude varies
even along one wavefront.
**Why not frequency or period.** These are the **same everywhere** in the medium, not
just on one wavefront ✓ A definition that applied to every point of the medium would
pick out no particular surface - which is why neither can be the defining property.
**Huygens' construction.** Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary
**wavelets**, and the new wavefront is their common tangent ✓ From this one idea follow
the laws of reflection and refraction, and the whole of diffraction theory.
**Why the idea is so useful.** It replaces tracking countless individual particles with
following a single surface ✓ Reflection, refraction, interference and diffraction are
all most naturally described in terms of what happens to wavefronts.
**What a lens does to one.** It converts an incoming **plane** wavefront into a
**converging spherical** one centred on the focus ✓ the wave-optics statement of "a lens
brings parallel rays to a point".
**The link to rays.** A ray is simply the **normal** to the wavefront ✓ Ray optics is
the limit of wave optics when the wavelength is negligible compared with the apparatus.
∴ phase.

Starting from the mean position, the displacement is **A sin ωt**; solve for t.
**Step 1 — write the displacement.** Measuring time from the mean position,
x = A sin ωt ✓
with A = **0·2 m** and
ω = 2π/T = 2π/24 = **π/12 rad s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute x = 0·1 m.**
0·1 = 0·2 sin(πt/12)
**sin(πt/12) = 0·5** ✓
**Step 3 — solve.**
πt/12 = π/6
**t = 2 s** ✓
**Why the answer is not T/4 or anything so large.** The point 0·1 m out is only
**halfway** to the extreme, and near the mean position the particle is moving at its
**fastest** ✓ so it covers the first half of the amplitude very quickly - in 2 s out of
the 6 s it takes to reach the extreme.
**The timings across a quarter cycle.**
to x = A/2 (0·1 m): **2 s** ✓
to x = A/√2 (0·141 m): **3 s**
to x = A√3/2 (0·173 m): **4 s**
to x = A (0·2 m): **6 s** ✓
The particle takes 2 s for the first half of the amplitude and 4 s for the second - the
motion slows dramatically as it approaches the turning point.
**The speed at that point.**
v = ω√(A² − x²) = (π/12)√(0·04 − 0·01) = **0·045 m s⁻¹** ✓
against a maximum of ωA = **0·052 m s⁻¹** at the centre - still 86% of full speed, which
is why it got there so quickly.
**Why sine and not cosine.** The clock starts at the **mean** position, where x = 0 ✓
sin 0 = 0, so sine is the right function. Starting from an **extreme** would call for
x = A cos ωt.
**A useful landmark.** The particle is at **half amplitude** after **T/12** ✓ Here
24/12 = 2 s - a result worth remembering, since A/2 occurs so often in SHM questions.
**Reading the distractors.** **3 s** ✗ is the time to A/√2. **12 s** ✗ is half a period,
by which time the particle is back at the mean position moving the other way. **8 s** ✗
corresponds to x = 0·173 m going on past ✓
∴ 2 s.

Uniform circular motion repeats, so it is **periodic** - but the restoring force is not
proportional to a displacement along a line, so it is not **SHM**.
**Step 1 — test for periodicity.** The particle returns to the same position with the
same velocity after each revolution, at regular intervals T = 2πr/v ✓ So the motion is
**periodic**.
**Step 2 — test for simple harmonic motion.** SHM requires
**a = −ω²x** ✓
a **linear** restoring acceleration directed towards a fixed point on a **straight
line**. In circular motion the acceleration is ω²r in magnitude - **constant**, not
proportional to any displacement - and the motion is two-dimensional, not along a line.
So it is **not SHM** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The motion is **periodic but not SHM** ✓
**The relationship between the two.** **Every** SHM is periodic, but not every periodic
motion is SHM ✓ SHM is the special case in which the restoring force is **directly
proportional to the displacement** and oppositely directed.
**The beautiful connection, though.** The **projection** of uniform circular motion onto
any **diameter** is exact SHM ✓
x = r cos ωt
with a = −ω²x precisely. This is why the **phasor** or reference-circle construction
is so useful for SHM, and why ω appears in both.
**Other periodic motions that are not SHM.**
the Earth's orbit around the Sun ✓
a bouncing ball
a pendulum swinging through a **large** angle - SHM only for small amplitudes, where
sin θ ≈ θ ✓
**Why the small-angle condition matters for a pendulum.** The restoring torque goes as
sin θ, which is proportional to θ only for small angles ✓ At 30° the error is about
1·7%, and at 90° the motion is distinctly non-sinusoidal.
**Why "neither periodic nor SHM" is wrong.** The particle plainly repeats its motion ✓
A motion that is not periodic would be something like a projectile's flight or a
spiral.
**Why "SHM but not periodic" is impossible.** SHM is sinusoidal and therefore
necessarily periodic ✓ The option is self-contradictory.
∴ periodic but not SHM.
